column1: In digital painting, are you mixing physical pigments or manipulating emitted light?
column2: Emitted light — RGB models directly manipulate intensities of red (~630nm), green (~532nm), and blue (~465nm) emissive phosphors/LEDs, unlike reflective pigment mixing.

column1: What are the three types of cone photoreceptors in the human retina, and what do they respond to?
column2: S (short-wavelength, blue-sensitive), M (medium-wavelength, green-sensitive), and L (long-wavelength, red-sensitive) cones — they respond as overlapping bell-curve sensitivities, not discrete categorical bins.

column1: Why does 'yellow' appear in human color perception if there is no dedicated yellow photoreceptor?
column2: Yellow emerges when M and L cones are stimulated simultaneously while the S cone remains relatively quiet — it's a product of combined cone response, not a single receptor.

column1: What is metamerism, and why does it matter for digital painters?
column2: Metamerism is when physically distinct spectral distributions appear as the same color to the eye. It matters because colors may match on one display/print but mismatch on another, affecting proofing across devices.

column1: Name the three perceptual dimensions into which all color can be decomposed.
column2: Hue (dominant wavelength/color identity), Saturation (purity/chroma), and Value/Lightness (total light energy from black to white).

column1: What key limitation does HSV/HSL color space have despite being perceptually intuitive?
column2: It is mathematically non-uniform — equal numerical steps in hue, saturation, or value do not correspond to equal perceptual differences.

column1: What are the three pillars of spatial coherence in figure/form construction?
column2: Projection Geometry (3D-to-2D perspective mapping), Proportion Frameworks (measurable figure ratios, e.g., 8-head canon), and skeletal-muscular anatomical logic.

column1: What is the core architectural invariant separating all digital brush systems?
column2: The separation of brush shape geometry (grayscale bitmap defining pigment footprint) from brush dynamics parameters (pressure, tilt, velocity, jitter) that modulate that shape in real time.

column1: Why do professional brush engines use non-linear (Bézier spline) pressure curves instead of linear mapping?
column2: Because human motor control perceives force logarithmically, not linearly — light touches feel exponentially more delicate while hard presses plateau in perceived intensity, so a configurable curve better matches perception.

column1: What is the target end-to-end latency budget for real-time digital painting responsiveness, and the tighter professional target?
column2: Approximately 16ms at 60fps for standard real-time feedback; professional workflows target ~8ms at 120Hz to eliminate perceptual lag between hand motion and visual feedback.

column1: What is the first compositional invariant regarding visual weight?
column2: Visual weight is not synonymous with physical area — it emerges from color saturation, value contrast, texture density, edge sharpness, and spatial position within the frame.

column1: How does compositional 'dynamic equilibrium' differ from mathematical/symmetrical balance?
column2: Dynamic equilibrium arises from mutual tension between unequal visual weights positioned in opposition (e.g., a small intense element balancing a larger subtle one), rather than mirrored symmetrical division of the frame.
